Stage 1 · ANALYZE — Teacher Manual
About
This
Teacher
Manual
This manual provides the complete instructional architecture for Stage 1: ANALYZE of the Jurassic Thinking
Cycle™. It is intended for licensed Jurassic English™ educators and should be read in conjunction with the
Teacher & Curriculum Guidebook v3.0 (World Wise Learning, 2026).
The
Four
Commitments
of
a
Jurassic
English™
Teacher
1. Intellectual integrity: Never accept opinion without evidence; never answer your own question; never simplify a text to
remove diﬃculty.
2. Structural discipline: All four Cycle stages present in every lesson; no stage skipped; no lesson ends without a Reﬂect
prompt.
3. Relational attunement: Read regulation cues before demanding output; know your students’ emotional baseline; never
shame intellectual struggle.
4. Ecological responsibility: Model eco-reasoning language; incorporate ecological reﬂection at Level 3+; connect
literature to the living world.
Stage
Architecture
Parameter Speciﬁcation
Stage Number 1
Stage Name ANALYZE
Cognitive Operation Deconstruction of textual elements to establish objective understanding.
Bloom’s Taxonomy Level 3 (Analysis)
Primary Target Deconstruct
Lesson Slot (40-min model) 5–15 min
Primary Activity Guided close reading; teacher models with think-aloud
Assessment Type Observation
Assessment Form Circulate; note which students identify implicit vs. explicit
Teacher Action Prompt or redirect with clariﬁcation questions
Learning
Objectives
By the end of a well-executed lesson at this stage, students will demonstrate the following measurable
behaviours. Objectives apply across all ﬁve series levels; the complexity of evidence and language varies by
CEFR band.
1. Identify characters, setting, and plot events with textual grounding
2. Distinguish explicitly stated information from implicit inference

Standards
Alignment
CEFR: Mapped to B1–C1 reasoning descriptors (Appendix D, Teacher Guidebook v3.0)
CCSS: Aligned to anchor standards for reading, writing, and speaking (Appendix E)
Bloom’s Taxonomy: Level 3 (Analysis) — TARGET: Deconstruct
UNESCO ESD: Integrated at Level 3+ through the Ecocentric Reasoning Extension (Section 19)
Master
Prompt
Bank
Questions in Jurassic English™ are classiﬁed by cognitive demand. Recall and comprehension questions
(Bloom’s Levels 1–2) function as scaﬀolding only. The target zone for all lessons is Bloom’s Levels 3–6, mapped
to the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ stages.
Prompt
Type Example
Prompt Purpose
Elicitation 'What is happening in this scene?' Establish baseline comprehension
Clariﬁcation 'What evidence shows the character is afraid?' Distinguish observation from inference
Structural 'How does the author organise this information?' Reveal craft moves and authorial
intention
Ecological 'What does the setting tell us about the relationship
between the characters and their environment?'
Surface ecological and environmental
dimensions
Accountable
Talk
Moves
These teacher moves are used speciﬁcally at the Analyze stage to push reasoning quality and maintain
intellectual accountability.
Move Teacher
Language Purpose
Challenging 'What in the text supports that?' Push for evidence
Pressing 'Say more about why that matters.' Deepen the observation
Revoicing 'So you are saying that… Is that right?' Clarify and validate
Eco-Pressing 'What does this mean for the living world beyond the
story?'
Extend to ecological reﬂection
Prohibited
Dialogue
Practices
(Section
8.3,
Guidebook
v3.0)
Never answer your own question: wait 7 seconds; rephrase; pair-share ﬁrst.
Never accept ‘I don’t know’ without pressing: ‘Take a guess. What might be one reason?’
Never praise content-free responses. Mark the reasoning instead: ‘That was a analyze because…’

Philosophy
(Section
9.1,

v3.0)
Jurassic English™ assesses the logic of the reasoning link, not merely the presence of a quotation.
A student who cites evidence but cannot explain the connection between evidence and claim has not yet demonstrated
proﬁcient reasoning.
The rubric is shared with students before instruction begins and used consistently for both formative and summative
purposes.

Provide sentence frame; model the
missing component; require re-attempt
before moving on.

without explicit citation; limited inference.
Press for the missing component by
name. Identify exactly what is absent.
3 — Proﬁcient Clearly distinguishes explicit from implicit; locates
purposeful evidence; identiﬁes author craft choices.
Mark publicly; identify the speciﬁc
strength; oﬀer a stretch prompt.
4 — Advanced Analyses multiple layers (character, craft, ecology);
challenges surface readings; identiﬁes subtext and
authorial intent.
Use as a model for class discussion;
ask the student to teach the structure to
a peer.

Stage 1 · ANALYZE — Student Manual
How
to
Use
This
Manual
This manual is your personal reference guide for Stage 1: ANALYZE of the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™. Use it
before, during, and after lessons to understand what this stage requires, access the academic language you
need, practise with graduated prompts, and assess your own progress.
Keep
this
manual
in
your
reading
portfolio.
Your
teacher
will
refer
to
it
during
lessons.
The
sentence
frames
in
Section
4
are
available
for
all
written
and
oral
tasks.
Your
Place
in
the
Thinking
Cycle
The Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ has four stages. You will complete all four in every lesson. No stage may be
skipped.
Stage What
You
Do Your
Position
01 ANALYZE Break the text apart. Find evidence. Identify what is really there. ►  YOU ARE HERE
02
EVALUATE
Make a judgment. Apply a standard. Decide what matters.
03 JUSTIFY Build your argument. Claim + Evidence + Warrant + Impact.
04 REFLECT Connect the text to your life, the world, and the living world.
Stage
1:
ANALYZE
—
Your
Cognitive
Target
Cognitive Operation: Deconstruction of textual elements to establish objective understanding.
Bloom’s Level: 3 (Analysis) | Target: Deconstruct
What
Is
Analyze?
Deconstruction
of
textual
elements
to
establish
objective
understanding.
In the Jurassic English™ framework, Analyze is Stage 1 of the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™. It corresponds to
Bloom’s Taxonomy Level 3 (Analysis). Its primary target cognitive operation is: Deconstruct.
What
You
Are
Expected
to
Do
Identify characters, setting, and plot events with textual grounding
Distinguish explicitly stated information from implicit inference
Recognise narrative perspective and authorial craft choices
Note emotional and psychological states of characters with evidence
Identify ecological and environmental details embedded in the setting

Academic
Language
Bank
Use these sentence frames in spoken discussion and written work. They are scaﬀolds, not rules — adapt them
as your conﬁdence grows.
Function Sentence
Frame Use
This
When...
Analysis 'In this scene, ___ is happening.' Establish what occurs
Evidence 'The text states / shows / describes ___.' Ground claims in the text
Inference 'This suggests / implies that ___.' Move from explicit to implicit
Craft 'The author uses ___ to show ___.' Identify technique and eﬀect
Character 'The character feels / thinks / wants ___ because ___.' Internal state with textual grounding
Ecological 'The setting shows the relationship between ___ and
the environment by ___.'
Surface ecological dimension
Practice
Prompts
by
Level
Your teacher will select the appropriate prompt level for your series. You may also use prompts above your
current level as a stretch challenge.
Foundation
/
Development
(Pre-A1
to
A2)
Identify three facts about the main character directly from the text. What does the character do in this scene?
What words tell you how the character is feeling?
Expansion
/
Mastery
(A2
to
B2)
What evidence shows the character's motivation? How does the author use language to reveal internal conﬂict?
What does the setting contribute to the mood?
Advanced
(B2
to
C1)
Analyse the narrative perspective and its eﬀect on reader interpretation. What is the author's craft move in this
passage? How does the ecological setting function as more than background detail?
